result:
Solution 2 has the correct answer. The condition means every pair of vertices has at least two common neighbours, and the minimum number of edges is $S(n)=\lceil(5n-8)/2\rceil$.

**Lower bound.** Every vertex has degree at least 3, since a degree-2 vertex can share at most one common neighbour with one of its neighbours. Let $v$ have minimum degree $\delta$. Counting common neighbours of $v$ with all other vertices gives $\sum_{w\in N(v)}(d_w-1)\ge 2(n-1)$. Bounding the degrees of the remaining vertices by $\delta$ gives $2m\ge 2(n-1)+\delta(n+1-\delta)$. For $\delta=3$ this is $2m\ge 5n-8$. The cases $\delta\ge 4$ also satisfy $2m\ge 5n-8$, and the complete graph is far above the bound.

**Construction.** For even $n$, take two adjacent hubs joined to all other vertices, plus a perfect matching on the remaining $n-2$ vertices. This has $(5n-8)/2$ edges and every pair has at least two common neighbours. For odd $n$, add a vertex to the even construction on $n-1$ vertices, joined to both hubs and one matched vertex. This adds 3 edges and reaches $(5n-7)/2=\lceil(5n-8)/2\rceil$. Solution 2's own construction fails for odd $n$, but its formula is still right.

**Sum.** The values for $n=10,\dots,20$ are $21, 24, 26, 29, 31, 34, 36, 39, 41, 44, 46$, which total $371$.

Solution 1 uses a weaker bound and wrong values, and Solution 3's formulas are inconsistent with $S(5)=9$ and too large.

CHOICE: 2
